title: Arriving in New York in 1964 prepared: college, Army band practice and first recordings
summary: McBee says he needed no mentor beyond Paul Chambers; he studied classics, practiced bass in the Army and arrived to record with Moncur, Jackie McLean and Charles Lloyd.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Well as you said, your older guys who have been around, when you moved to New York in 1964, I think I’m correct about that, I’m going to guess that as a jazz musician you had to do a certain amount of scrambling, reaching out to other people, finding a mentor, and making connections. Isn’t that part of finding out who you are, forming your personality. And I wonder if young people don’t have that opportunity now?

Young people don’t have a lot of that kind of opportunity, but as far as I’m concerned, when I arrived in New York City I needed not a sound. I had no need for a mentor. I had no need to discover myself. I had, although having not researched who was doing what at what level, etcetera, etcetera. I had studied. I wanted to be a music teacher. So I finished college before arriving in New York and I tell everybody that in college I flunked everything but I was a great student in the music area. And so when I arrived in New York City I was very, very abreast of what music was. I studied the classics, Bach, Beethoven, you know, Stravinsky etcetera, etcetera, Schoenberg. Paul Chambers was my greatest mentor so far as being in, as a young guy in need of some kind of guidance — you know listening to him was my world. And through my serious study of the

instrument, I mean I was in the Army before I finished college, in the band, as a clarinetist. And when the band practices were finished, for two years, I would practice my bass throughout the waning, the late hours of the evening, on and on. You know I had this inspiration to develop my personal reality. So doing that for two years, then returning to college, finishing, graduating with a degree in music education, when I arrived in New York City I felt I had something on my shoulder. And upon listening to those around me, with the exception of a few, I mean I felt very competitive if you will. Because I heard a lot of it all. I felt rather comfortable with myself as one who would express at my expected level of competence. And that happened. Because the moment I arrived in New York City, my first record was with Grachan Moncur III called “Some Other Stuff” which featured Herbie Hancock, Wayne Shorter and Tony Williams. And then I went from there to Jackie McLean, and then I went from there to Charles Lloyd. You know, and I’m just arriving in New York. So I felt pretty good about my entrance into the city.
